q: This kind of diagram uses overlapping circles to show relationships between sets. The overlap represents elements that belong to both sets. It is named for a British logician. For 10 points, name this diagram.

This one-sided surface can be made by giving a strip of paper a half twist and joining the ends. If you cut it down the middle you get one longer loop. It is named for a German mathematician. For 10 points, name this surface, whose name resembles a "strip."

This number is about 1.618 and is the positive solution to x squared equals x plus one. The ratio of consecutive Fibonacci numbers approaches it. Artists claim it appears in the Parthenon. For 10 points, name this ratio, represented by the Greek letter phi.

This concept is the idea of something without any bound. The symbol for it resembles a sideways figure eight and was introduced by John Wallis. Georg Cantor showed that there are different sizes of it. For 10 points, name this concept.

A positive integer is this kind of number if it equals the sum of its proper divisors. Six, which equals 1 plus 2 plus 3, is the smallest one. The next is 28. For 10 points, name this kind of number, which Euclid linked to Mersenne primes.

Eratosthenes devised a method named for this object to find primes. One crosses out the multiples of each prime in a list, leaving only the primes. For 10 points, give the household item in the name of this algorithm that "filters" numbers.

These are real numbers that cannot be written as a ratio of two integers. The square root of 2 is the classic example, which a Pythagorean legend says was proved by Hippasus. Their decimals never end or repeat. For 10 points, name this type of number, contrasted with rational ones.
Answer these questions about polygons.
parts: What polygon has five sides?
What polygon has eight sides, like a stop sign?
What is the sum, in degrees, of the interior angles of any quadrilateral?

q: Answer these questions about geometry terms.
parts: What kind of angle measures more than 90 degrees but less than 180 degrees?
What term describes two lines in a plane that never intersect?
What term describes a line that touches a circle at exactly one point?

q: Answer these questions about kinds of numbers.
parts: What term describes the whole numbers and their negatives, such as minus 3, 0, and 5?
What is the term for the distance of a number from zero on the number line, written with vertical bars?
What is the multiplicative inverse of a number, such as one third for the number 3?

q: Answer these questions about famous mathematicians.
parts: Which Greek mathematician from Syracuse estimated pi using polygons and discovered the volume of a sphere?
Which German mathematician, called the mother of modern algebra, proved a theorem linking symmetries and conservation laws?
Which Indian mathematician, born in 1887, produced thousands of formulas and collaborated with G. H. Hardy?

q: Answer these questions about algebra.
parts: What is the name for a letter, like x, that stands for an unknown number?
What is the term for the number multiplied by the letter in a term, such as the 4 in 4x?
What Persian scholar's name is the origin of the word algorithm and whose book gave algebra its name?

q: Answer these questions about statistics.
parts: What is the difference between the largest and smallest values in a data set?
What is the name for a data point that lies far from the rest of the data?
What measure of spread is the square root of the variance?

q: Answer these questions about area and volume.
parts: What shape has an area given by pi times radius squared?
What is the volume, in cubic units, of a cube with sides of length 3?
What 3D shape has the formula four-thirds times pi times the radius cubed for its volume?

q: Answer these questions about the history of numbers.
parts: Which ancient civilization of Mesopotamia used a base-60 number system, which we still use for minutes and seconds?
What calculating tool, with beads on rods, was used in ancient times in Asia and Europe?
What system of ten digits, developed in India and transmitted by Arabic scholars, is used worldwide today?

q: This is a step-by-step set of instructions for solving a problem or completing a task. A recipe is a familiar everyday example of one. Programmers measure how efficient these are by how their running time grows with input size. For 10 points, name this term for a precise procedure, whose name derives from al-Khwarizmi.

Place values in this number system are powers of two, so the decimal number 5 is written as 101. Logic gates in processors operate on its digits. Its two symbols are often represented as true and false. For 10 points, name this number system that uses only 0 and 1.

This is a group of eight bits. It is the usual unit for storing a single character of text. A kilo- version of this unit is about a thousand of them. For 10 points, name this unit of digital information.

This popular programming language was created by Guido van Rossum and named for a British comedy group. It is known for readable code that uses indentation to mark blocks. It is widely used in data science and teaching. For 10 points, name this language, not a snake.

This is the markup language used to structure web pages. It uses tags such as paragraph and heading elements. Cascading Style Sheets are used with it to control appearance. For 10 points, give the four-letter acronym for this language, written by Tim Berners-Lee for hypertext documents.

This is the global network of networks that links billions of computers. It grew out of ARPANET, a project funded by the United States Department of Defense. Email and the World Wide Web both run on it. For 10 points, name this network.

In programming, this structure repeats a block of code until a condition is met or for a set number of times. For and while are common kinds. Without a way to stop it, one of these can run forever. For 10 points, name this structure.

Often called the "brain" of the computer, this component executes program instructions. Its speed is measured in gigahertz, and Intel and AMD make many models. It carries out the fetch, decode, and execute cycle. For 10 points, name this component, abbreviated CPU.

This is the temporary memory a computer uses to store data and programs currently in use. Its contents are lost when the power is turned off. Adding more of it can help a computer run multiple programs. For 10 points, name this kind of memory, abbreviated RAM.

Windows, macOS, and Android are examples of this type of software. It manages hardware, runs applications, and provides a user interface. Without it, a computer cannot run programs like word processors. For 10 points, name this system software, abbreviated OS.

This is the smallest controllable element of a picture on a digital screen. A typical image is made up of a grid of thousands or millions of them. The word is a blend of "picture" and "element." For 10 points, name this unit.

Chrome, Firefox, and Safari are examples of this type of software. It retrieves web pages from servers and displays them. Users type addresses into its address bar. For 10 points, name this kind of program used to surf the web.

This English mathematician proposed the Turing machine and helped break the German Enigma code during World War II. A famous test of machine intelligence is named for him, and the Association for Computing Machinery's highest award bears his name. For 10 points, name this man.

This woman, a daughter of Lord Byron, wrote notes on Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine that include a method for calculating Bernoulli numbers. She is often called an early computer programmer. For 10 points, name this English mathematician.

This British scientist invented the World Wide Web in 1989 while working at CERN. He wrote the first web browser and server. He proposed HTTP and URLs. For 10 points, name this computer scientist, whose name includes "Berners."

This American rear admiral and computer scientist developed the first compiler and helped create COBOL. She is associated with the story of a moth found in the Harvard Mark II. For 10 points, name this woman, nicknamed "Amazing Grace."

This English mathematician designed the Difference Engine and the Analytical Engine. He is sometimes called the "father of the computer" even though his machines were never completed in his lifetime. Ada Lovelace worked with him. For 10 points, name this inventor.

This is a free, open-source operating system kernel created by Linus Torvalds in 1991. It powers Android phones, most web servers, and supercomputers. Its mascot is a penguin named Tux. For 10 points, name this operating system kernel.

This is a data structure that stores a collection of items in numbered positions. Most languages start counting positions at zero. Elements are accessed by their index. For 10 points, name this basic structure, a list of values of the same type.

This type of program translates source code written in a language like C into machine code that a processor can run. Grace Hopper wrote an early one. It differs from an interpreter, which runs code line by line. For 10 points, name this program.

This is an organized collection of structured data, typically managed with software and queried with SQL. Banks, libraries, and online stores use them to store records. For 10 points, name this system, where tables hold rows and columns.

This is a type of harmful software designed to damage or gain unauthorized access to computers. Viruses, worms, ransomware, and spyware are all kinds. Antivirus programs try to detect it. For 10 points, name this category of software.

This security system monitors and controls network traffic based on rules and can block unauthorized connections. It may be hardware or software. Its name comes from a wall that stops the spread of a blaze. For 10 points, name this protective system.

The scientist Douglas Engelbart demonstrated this pointing device in 1968 in a presentation later called "The Mother of All Demos." It moves a cursor on screen and has buttons that you click. For 10 points, name this input device whose name comes from a small rodent.
This is a numeric label, such as 192.168.1.1, that identifies a device on a network. Versions 4 and 6 are the main formats. Routers use it to deliver packets. For 10 points, name this address.

This is a data type with only two possible values, true and false. It is named for an English mathematician who developed a system of algebraic logic in 1854. AND, OR, and NOT are operations on it. For 10 points, give this term, named for a nineteenth-century mathematician from Lincoln, England.

This standard assigns numbers to letters and symbols; for example, 65 stands for uppercase A. It uses 7 bits to represent 128 characters. Unicode extended it to cover many more scripts. For 10 points, name this character encoding standard.

This observation made by a co-founder of Intel in 1965 states that the number of transistors on a chip roughly doubles about every two years. It has guided the semiconductor industry for decades. For 10 points, name this "law" named for Gordon.

This technique has a function call itself on a smaller version of the same problem until reaching a base case. Computing a factorial and traversing a tree are standard examples. For 10 points, name this programming technique, a joke about which is that you must first understand it.

This model of computing delivers services like storage and software over the internet from remote data centers rather than from a local machine. Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Azure are major providers. For 10 points, name this model, symbolized by a fluffy weather feature.
Answer these questions about the parts of a computer.
parts: What permanent storage device inside many computers holds files on spinning platters or flash memory?
What is the main circuit board that connects the CPU, memory, and other components?
What does the abbreviation GPU stand for, a chip that is specialized for rendering images?

parts: What block-based visual language, developed at MIT, is widely used to teach children to code?
What language, with a name that misleadingly suggests a coffee drink, adds interactivity to web pages?

q: Answer these questions about the web.
parts: What three-letter acronym names the address of a web page, such as one beginning with https?
What symbol separates the username from the domain in an email address?
What protocol, abbreviated HTTPS, adds encryption to web traffic? Give the missing word that "S" represents.

q: Answer these questions about data representation.
parts: How many bits are in one byte?
What is the number base used in the binary system?
What number system, with digits 0 to 9 and letters A to F, is commonly used to write colors and memory addresses?

q: Answer these questions about technology companies and their founders.
parts: Which co-founder of Apple introduced the iPhone in 2007?
Which co-founder of Microsoft, with Paul Allen, started the company in 1975?
Which Harvard student co-founded Facebook in 2004?

parts: What name is given to a named container that stores a value in a program?
What kind of statement runs code only if a condition is true, as in "if x is greater than 5"?
What is the name for a reusable block of code that can be called by name and may return a value?

q: Answer these questions about computer security.
parts: What term describes fraudulent emails that trick people into giving up passwords?
What is the process of scrambling data so that only someone with a key can read it?
What type of malware secretly gathers information about a user's activity?

q: Answer these questions about the history of computing.
parts: What electronic computer, completed in 1945 at the University of Pennsylvania, was designed to compute artillery tables?
What small semiconductor device replaced the vacuum tube in computers?
What early textile machine used punched cards to control weaving patterns, inspiring later computers?

q: When this quantity rises, each dollar buys fewer goods, which is why your grandparents remember much cheaper movie tickets. It is commonly measured by the Consumer Price Index. Central banks often aim to keep it low and steady, at around two percent per year. For 10 points, name this general rise in prices over time.

This concept states that people have unlimited wants but only limited resources to satisfy them. It forces every society to answer the questions of what to produce, how to produce it, and for whom. Time, money, and land are all examples of things that have it. For 10 points, name this basic economic problem of limited resources.

When the price of a good rises, producers are usually willing to offer more of it for sale. This relationship is shown by an upward-sloping line on a graph with price on the vertical axis. Together with its counterpart for buyers, it determines market price. For 10 points, name this half of a famous two-curve model, which is the amount of a good that sellers offer.

The law of this concept says that, all else equal, when the price of a good rises, the quantity people buy falls. Its curve slopes downward on a graph. Shifts in income, tastes, and the prices of related goods can move the whole curve. For 10 points, name this economic term for how much of a good consumers are willing and able to buy.

A famous example of this idea is that attending college means giving up the wages you could earn at a full-time job. Economists say every choice has one, and it is the value of the next best alternative that you give up. For 10 points, name this concept that is the real price of any decision beyond the money spent.

It is measured by adding up consumption, investment, government spending, and net exports. Simon Kuznets helped develop it in the 1930s. When economists say an economy is growing, they usually mean this figure is rising after adjusting for inflation. For 10 points, name this measure of the total value of goods and services produced within a country, abbreviated G-D-P.

In this kind of market, one firm is the only seller of a product and has no close substitutes. Examples have included a local water utility and, historically, Standard Oil. Because there is no competition, the firm can charge higher prices. For 10 points, name this market structure with a single seller.

Economists often define this event as two consecutive quarters of falling gross domestic product. During it, businesses cut back, unemployment rises, and consumers spend less. A particularly deep and long one is called a depression. For 10 points, name this downturn in economic activity.

This Scottish thinker wrote that a butcher, brewer, and baker serve us out of self-interest rather than benevolence. He described how a division of labor in a pin factory raises productivity. He published a 1776 book on the causes of national prosperity. For 10 points, name this author of The Wealth of Nations.

Established in 1913, this institution has a Board of Governors in Washington and twelve regional banks. It sets monetary policy by buying and selling government securities, and it acts as lender of last resort to banks. For 10 points, name this central bank of the United States, often shortened to the Fed.

This type of tax is placed on goods imported from other countries, which makes foreign products more expensive in the domestic market. The Smoot-Hawley one of 1930 is a famous example. Supporters say it protects domestic industries. For 10 points, name this tax on imports.

People are counted in this category if they are without a job but are actively looking for work. The Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes a monthly rate for it. A person who has stopped looking, called a discouraged worker, is not counted. For 10 points, name this condition of being jobless, which rose sharply during the Great Depression.

This British economist argued in a 1936 book that governments should increase spending during downturns to boost demand. His ideas influenced the New Deal and the Bretton Woods conference. He wrote The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money. For 10 points, name this economist whose name labels a school of thought.

David Ricardo illustrated this principle with the example of wine from Portugal and cloth from England. It holds that countries should specialize in what they produce at the lowest opportunity cost, even if another country is better at everything. For 10 points, name this principle that explains the gains from trade.

Owning a share of this means owning a small piece of a corporation. Its price is shown on tickers on exchanges like the Nasdaq. Owners may receive dividends. For 10 points, give this term for a unit of ownership in a company, which is bought and sold on markets.

This is the price of borrowing money, expressed as a percentage of the amount borrowed. When it falls, mortgages and car loans become cheaper and spending tends to rise. The Federal Reserve influences it through its federal funds target. For 10 points, name this cost of a loan.

This decade-long period began after the stock market crash of 1929. Unemployment in the United States reached about a quarter of workers, and thousands of banks failed. Franklin Roosevelt responded with the New Deal. For 10 points, name this worst economic downturn of the twentieth century.

OPEC members are often cited as an example of this market structure, in which a few large firms dominate, so each one's choices affect the others. Airlines and wireless carriers in many countries show it. Game theory, including the prisoner's dilemma, is often used to analyze it. For 10 points, name this market with only a handful of sellers.

Congress and the President use this tool by changing taxes and government spending. During a recession, a government might cut taxes or build highways to stimulate the economy. The other main tool, controlled by the central bank, is monetary policy. For 10 points, name this type of policy involving a government's budget.

This University of Chicago economist advocated that the money supply grow at a steady rate. He won the 1976 Nobel Prize and wrote Capitalism and Freedom. He was a leading monetarist and critic of Keynes. For 10 points, name this economist.

This is the opposite of inflation: a general fall in prices across the economy. It can seem good for shoppers, but it can cause people to delay purchases and make debts harder to repay. Japan struggled with it for years in the 1990s. For 10 points, name this decline in the general price level.

Economists measure this property using a ratio of the percentage change in quantity to the percentage change in price. Gasoline is considered to have low values of it in the short run, while luxury goods have high ones. When it is less than one, the good is described as inelastic. For 10 points, name this property that describes how sensitive buyers are to price changes.

A country has this when the value of its imports exceeds the value of its exports. The United States has had one with China for decades. It is part of the current account. For 10 points, name this imbalance in international trade, the opposite of a surplus.

This occurs in a year when a government spends more money than it collects in revenue. It is financed by borrowing, and the total of past ones forms the national debt. For 10 points, name this gap between spending and revenue in a government budget.

In this system of exchange, people trade goods or services directly without using money. It required a double coincidence of wants, which made trading difficult and led to the invention of currency. For 10 points, name this practice of swapping one good for another.

This word was coined to describe the 1970s American combination of rising unemployment and high inflation, which seemed impossible under older theories. It was triggered partly by oil price shocks from OPEC. For 10 points, name this portmanteau for stagnant growth plus inflation.

On a graph, this is the point where the supply and demand curves cross. At the price named for it, the quantity that buyers want exactly matches the quantity that sellers offer, so there is neither a shortage nor a surplus. For 10 points, give this two-word term, which includes a word meaning balance.

This French-derived word names a person who starts a new business and takes on its financial risk. Steve Jobs and Henry Ford are famous examples. They organize land, labor, and capital to make a product. For 10 points, name this type of business founder.

Adam Smith used this phrase for the way individuals pursuing their own self-interest in free markets end up helping society as a whole, as if guided by something unseen. It appears in The Wealth of Nations and is a key idea of laissez-faire thinking. For 10 points, give this two-word phrase.

This German philosopher co-wrote The Communist Manifesto with Friedrich Engels and also wrote Das Kapital. He criticized capitalism and argued that workers would eventually overthrow the owners of the means of production. For 10 points, name this thinker whose economic theories inspired communism.

This principle states that as you add more of one input, such as workers in a fixed-size factory, each additional unit eventually adds less extra output than the one before. Too many cooks in a small kitchen illustrates it. For 10 points, give this principle of declining marginal output, named for what happens to returns.

What term describes a loan from a bank used to buy a house, with the house itself serving as collateral?
What term names the money a bank is required to hold in reserve rather than lend, expressed as a percentage of deposits?

What term names a government payment to a business or industry meant to lower its costs and encourage production?
What term names a legal maximum price, such as a cap on rent, that is set below the equilibrium price?

q: Answer these questions about types of economic systems.

What term describes an economy in which the government makes most decisions about production and prices, as in the Soviet Union?
What term describes a system that mixes private enterprise with government regulation, as in most modern countries?

parts: What is the term for the money a worker earns per hour of work?
What name is given to an organization of workers that bargains with employers for pay and benefits?
What term is given to a legal minimum hourly pay that employers must provide, which the Fair Labor Standards Act first set in 1938?

parts: What factor of production includes natural resources such as soil, minerals, and forests?
What factor of production refers to the tools, machinery, and factories used to produce goods?
Which factor of production refers to the effort supplied by workers, whether physical or mental?

What name is given to a limit on the quantity of a good that may be imported, which is an alternative to a tariff?
Which international body, founded in 1995 and based in Geneva, replaced the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade?

q: Answer these questions about personal finance.
parts: What term names money set aside for future use, often in a bank account earning interest?
What term for a number from 300 to 850 estimates how likely a borrower is to repay debts?
What term names the practice of spreading investments across many assets to reduce risk, as in not putting all eggs in one basket?

q: This scientist trained dogs to salivate at the sound of a bell by repeatedly pairing the bell with food. He was a Russian physiologist who won the 1904 Nobel Prize for work on digestion. For 10 points, name this researcher who discovered classical conditioning.

This Austrian physician founded psychoanalysis and wrote The Interpretation of Dreams. He proposed that the mind has an id, ego, and superego. He used the technique of free association with patients on a couch. For 10 points, name this psychologist.

This process is the mental storing and later retrieving of information. Types include short-term, long-term, and working. Hermann Ebbinghaus studied how quickly forgetting happens on a curve named for him. For 10 points, name this mental ability, which is lost in amnesia.

This psychologist ranked human needs in a pyramid, with physiological needs at the base and self-actualization at the top. He is associated with humanistic psychology. For 10 points, name this American who proposed a hierarchy of needs.

A person with this condition may feel sad, lose interest in activities they once enjoyed, and have changes in sleep and appetite. It is a mood disorder often treated with therapy and medication. For 10 points, name this common mental illness, sometimes called a clinical form of being down.

The Stanford prison experiment was conducted by this psychologist, who also served as president of the American Psychological Association. Participants were assigned roles as guards and prisoners. For 10 points, name this researcher, first name Philip.

In this 1960s study, participants were told to give increasingly strong electric shocks to a learner when he answered incorrectly. Most continued to the highest level because a man in a lab coat told them to. For 10 points, name this Yale study of obedience to authority.

Most vivid ones occur during R-E-M sleep, when the eyes move quickly under the lids. Freud called them the royal road to the unconscious, and he wrote a famous book interpreting them. For 10 points, name these stories and images that the mind produces during sleep.

This part of the brain, shaped like a seahorse, is important for forming new long-term memories. Damage to it caused the famous patient H.M. to be unable to form new memories. For 10 points, name this structure in the limbic system.

This researcher showed children two identical glasses of water, poured one into a taller, thinner glass, and found that young children think the taller one holds more. Tests of this kind of conservation led him to describe stages of development. He was Swiss. For 10 points, name this man.

Psychologists use this term for the way people think they should handle a situation such as stress. Techniques for it include exercise, talking to friends, and deep breathing. For 10 points, name this word, which means managing difficult circumstances.

This term describes the strong emotional bond between an infant and caregiver. John Bowlby proposed a theory about it, and Mary Ainsworth tested it with the Strange Situation procedure. For 10 points, give this term.

The Rorschach test uses these shapes, which are meant to reveal how a person thinks. A person looks at symmetrical inkblots and says what they see. For 10 points, name this kind of test, in which people give open-ended answers to ambiguous images.

B. F. Skinner is known for this kind of learning, in which behavior is shaped by rewards and punishments. He used a box with a lever for rats. For 10 points, name this type of conditioning, named for how the subject acts on its environment.

This term was coined by Leon Festinger for the discomfort felt when a person holds two contradictory beliefs, or acts against their own beliefs. People often change an attitude to reduce it. For 10 points, name this psychological theory.

These disorders are marked by excessive fear or worry. Types include panic disorder, phobias, and generalized forms. For 10 points, name these disorders, which most commonly involve feeling nervous and afraid.

This is the part of the nervous system consisting of the brain and spinal cord. It processes information and sends commands to the rest of the body. For 10 points, give the two-word term, abbreviated C-N-S.

In Freud's theory, this part of the personality is the rational mediator that balances the demands of the id and the superego. It operates on the reality principle. For 10 points, name this part, whose Latin name means I.

This term describes the tendency to do worse at something in front of others, or the opposite. More generally, it names the influence of other people on individuals. For 10 points, name this field of psychology, which studies how people think about and act around other people.
This Swiss psychiatrist founded analytical psychology and developed ideas such as the collective unconscious and archetypes. He broke with Freud in 1913. For 10 points, name this man.

This disorder is often diagnosed in childhood. Symptoms include trouble paying attention, being very active, and acting without thinking. It is abbreviated A-D-H-D. For 10 points, give the full name of this disorder, whose first word is attention.

This 1950s experiment by Solomon Asch showed participants lines of different lengths and had actors give wrong answers. Many subjects went along with the group. For 10 points, name this kind of social pressure, shown in the Asch experiment.

This is the term for a prediction or belief that comes true because a person acts as if it were true. Robert Merton named it. The Pygmalion effect in classrooms is a version. For 10 points, name this kind of prophecy.

This test, developed by Alfred Binet and later revised at Stanford, produces a score meant to measure intelligence. The average score is set at 100. For 10 points, give the abbreviation or full name of this type of score.

This part of the brain, located at the back and below the cerebrum, coordinates balance and fine movement. Damage to it can cause clumsy, shaky walking known as ataxia. Its name is Latin for little brain. For 10 points, name this structure.

This term describes the unlearned tendency, such as sucking in newborns, to respond to certain stimuli. Unlike habits, these are automatic. For 10 points, name this type of inborn response, as when a doctor taps your knee.
This type of therapy, associated with Aaron Beck, helps patients identify and change unhelpful thoughts and behaviors. It is abbreviated C-B-T. For 10 points, name this common therapy.

In his 1960s experiment, Albert Bandura had children watch adults hit an inflatable clown. Children later copied the aggression. For 10 points, name this experiment named for a toy, which showed observational learning.
This is the mental state of being aware of oneself and the surroundings. It is lost during deep anesthesia. For 10 points, name this term, which William James described as a stream.

In medical and psychological trials, a sugar pill given to the control group is an example of this. People who take it often report feeling better simply because they expect to. For 10 points, name this inactive treatment, whose Latin name means I shall please.

q: This word names the shared beliefs, customs, language, food, art, and values of a group of people. Sociologists distinguish its material objects from its nonmaterial ideas. Anthropologists also study it, and it is passed from one generation to the next. For 10 points, name this learned way of life of a group.

This French sociologist wrote Suicide in 1897 and The Division of Labor in Society. He is considered one of the founders of the discipline and studied how social facts shape individual behavior. For 10 points, name this man who coined the term anomie.

This German sociologist wrote The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism. He wrote about bureaucracy and defined the state as holding a monopoly on legitimate force. For 10 points, name this man.

This is the lifelong process in which people learn the norms, values, and behaviors of their society. Families, schools, peer groups, and the media are agents of it. For 10 points, give this term for how individuals learn to function in society.

These are the unwritten rules about what behavior is expected in a given society or group. Examples include waiting in line, shaking hands on meeting, and not talking in a library. Folkways and mores are two types. For 10 points, name this term for standards of behavior.

This French thinker coined the word sociology and is often called the father of the field. He proposed that societies pass through theological, metaphysical, and positive stages. For 10 points, name this founder of positivism.

This term describes a person's position in the hierarchy of society based on wealth, education, and occupation. Common divisions include upper, middle, and working. For 10 points, name this concept, such as the middle one in the United States.

This English writer translated Auguste Comte into English and wrote Society in America after a trip to the United States. She is sometimes called the first woman sociologist. For 10 points, name this author of How to Observe Manners and Morals.

This African American scholar wrote The Souls of Black Folk, in which he described double consciousness. He co-founded the N-A-A-C-P and wrote the first case study of an African American community, The Philadelphia Negro. For 10 points, name this sociologist.

In sociology, behavior that violates social norms is given this name. Robert Merton and Howard Becker wrote about it, and it can range from minor rule breaking to crime. For 10 points, name this term, which includes labeling theory.

This term is used for an oversimplified and often unfair belief about all members of a group. Examples include assuming that all teenagers are lazy. For 10 points, give this word for a fixed generalization about people.

This group is defined by sociologists as a category of people who face unequal treatment based on traits such as race, religion, or ethnicity, which is not necessarily smaller than the dominant group. Louis Wirth defined it. For 10 points, name this term.

This is the study of human populations, including their size, age, density, and distribution. A census collects such data. For 10 points, give this term, whose name sounds like it is about people and graphs.
This term refers to the movement of people from rural areas into cities and the growth of urban populations. It accompanied the Industrial Revolution. For 10 points, name this process.

This is the phrase used by C. Wright Mills for the ability to see the link between personal troubles and larger social issues. It is also the title of his 1959 book. For 10 points, give this two-word phrase, which includes the faculty of picturing.

This type of family consists of two parents and their children living in a single household. It contrasts with the extended family that includes grandparents, aunts, and uncles. For 10 points, name this type of family.

This term refers to the set of behaviors expected of a person who holds a particular position, such as a teacher or a parent. People may experience conflict when they hold several. For 10 points, name this concept.
This term describes a group of people of similar age and interests who influence one another, especially in adolescence. For 10 points, name this group that includes your friends and classmates.

Erving Goffman wrote a 1963 book about this term, meaning a mark of social disgrace that makes a person discredited. Examples include a criminal record or a visible illness. For 10 points, name this term.

This type of society is based on large-scale machine production and factories, and it replaced agricultural societies in the nineteenth century. For 10 points, name this kind of society, which emerged after a revolution in Britain.
This term describes the ranking of people into layers or levels in society based on wealth, power, and prestige. Caste and class are two systems of it. For 10 points, name this term.
This rigid form of social stratification, long associated with India, assigns people by birth into hereditary groups such as Brahmins and Dalits. For 10 points, name this closed system.
This is an opinion or feeling about a person formed before knowing the facts, often negative and based on group membership. For 10 points, name this term, which includes racial and religious forms.
This term refers to the unfair treatment of people based on group membership, such as being denied a job because of race. It is the behavioral counterpart to prejudice. For 10 points, name this term.

This practice, ended by Brown versus Board of Education and the Civil Rights Act, involved the legally enforced separation of racial groups in schools and public places in the American South. For 10 points, name this system, enforced by Jim Crow laws.

This group within a larger culture has its own distinct values, slang, and styles, such as punks, goths, or surfers. Members often share music and fashion that set them apart from the mainstream. For 10 points, give this word, which includes a prefix meaning below.

This term describes the cultural and social roles, behaviors, and identities associated with being male or female, as distinct from biological sex. Sociologists say these expectations are learned and differ between societies, and Judith Butler and Simone de Beauvoir wrote about them. For 10 points, give this term.

This sociologist developed a theory called symbolic interactionism, building on the ideas of George Herbert Mead. His coined phrase is looking-glass self, describing how we see ourselves based on how others see us. For 10 points, name this American who wrote Human Nature and the Social Order.
This is the process of moving into a new country in order to live there permanently. Ellis Island processed millions of people doing it. For 10 points, name this term, the opposite of emigration.

This term describes a pattern in which a person's own group is treated as the standard, so that other cultures are judged by its values. William Graham Sumner coined it. For 10 points, give this term, which combines a word for a group of people with a word meaning center.
Answer these questions about the founders of sociology.
parts: Which Frenchman coined the word sociology?
Which German wrote about the iron cage of rationalization?
Which Englishman wrote Principles of Sociology and coined the phrase survival of the fittest?

q: Answer these questions about social groups.
parts: What term names the small, close group that raises children and provides care?
In sociology, what term describes a group to which you do not belong, as opposed to an in-group?
Which sociologist distinguished between primary groups and secondary groups, with the former being intimate and personal?

q: Answer these questions about population.
parts: What is the count of all people living in a country, taken in the United States every ten years?
What term names the number of births per thousand people in a population per year?
Which English economist warned in 1798 that population grows faster than food supply?

q: Answer these questions about research methods in sociology.
parts: What is the name for a set of questions given to many people to gather data about their opinions?
What research method involves a researcher living among the people being studied and watching what they do?
What term for a small portion of a population is chosen to represent the whole group being studied?

q: Answer these questions about education and society.
parts: What institution is the main place where children learn skills and socialization outside the home in modern society?
What term refers to the unspoken lessons, such as obedience and punctuality, that students learn in classrooms?
What term describes the degree to which people move up or down the class ladder?

q: Answer these questions about race and ethnicity.
parts: What word describes people who share a cultural heritage, language, and ancestry?
What term is used when a minority group is absorbed into the dominant culture and gives up its own?
What term describes a society in which many cultures coexist, as in the idea that is often compared to a salad bowl?

q: Answer these questions about theories in sociology.
parts: What is the name for the perspective of Karl Marx that focuses on class struggle?
Which perspective views society as a system of interdependent parts, like organs in a body, each performing a function?
Which sociologist coined the term conspicuous consumption in The Theory of the Leisure Class?

q: Answer these questions about social problems.
parts: What term describes the state of lacking enough money for basic needs?
What term names the loss of a sense of social norms, a condition discussed by Durkheim?
What term describes the condition of lacking a permanent place to live, a social problem addressed by shelters?

q: Answer these questions about the media and technology.
parts: What word describes channels such as television, newspapers, and the internet that reach large audiences?
Which Canadian wrote that the medium is the message?
What term, coined by McLuhan, describes the world connected by electronic media?

q: This is a form of government in which power is held by the people, who either vote directly or elect representatives. Ancient Athens is an early example. For 10 points, name this system whose name comes from the Greek words for people and rule.
This is the supreme law of the United States, written in 1787 in Philadelphia and signed on September 17. It established three branches of government. For 10 points, name this founding document.

This French thinker wrote The Spirit of the Laws and argued that government power should be divided among separate branches. His ideas influenced the framers of the United States Constitution. For 10 points, name this Enlightenment philosopher.

This English philosopher wrote Two Treatises of Government and argued that people have natural rights to life, liberty, and property. Thomas Jefferson was influenced by him. For 10 points, name this man.
This English philosopher wrote Leviathan, which argued that life without government would be solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short. He supported a strong sovereign. For 10 points, name this man.

This Swiss-born philosopher wrote The Social Contract, which begins with the line that man is born free but is everywhere in chains. His idea of the general will influenced the French Revolution. For 10 points, name this man.

This idea divides the power of government into legislative, executive, and judicial branches. Each does a different job, such as making, enforcing, or interpreting the laws. For 10 points, name this principle, a major feature of the United States Constitution.

This system divides power between a national government and state or regional governments. The United States, Canada, Germany, and Australia are examples. For 10 points, name this system, whose Tenth Amendment reserves powers to the states.

This system lets each branch of the United States government limit the powers of the others. An example is the President vetoing a bill passed by Congress. For 10 points, name this system, in which each branch restrains the others.
This is the power of a president to reject a bill passed by the legislature. In the United States, Congress can override it with a two-thirds vote in both houses. For 10 points, name this action.

In the United States Senate, this tactic is used to delay or block a vote by prolonged speaking, and ending it requires a three-fifths vote known as cloture. For 10 points, name this tactic, which Jimmy Stewart made famous in a movie about a senator named Smith.

This is the process by which the United States elects its president. Each state has a number of votes equal to its senators and representatives, and 270 are needed to win. For 10 points, name this system.
This is the highest court in the United States, which has nine justices. Its decisions include Marbury v. Madison, which established judicial review. For 10 points, name this court.
The first ten changes to the United States Constitution, ratified in 1791, are known by this collective name. They guarantee freedoms of speech and religion. For 10 points, give this name.
This is a government in which a king or queen is the head of state. Britain, Spain, and Japan are modern examples, and many are constitutional. For 10 points, name this form of government.

This is a form of government in which one leader holds complete power and often rules by force without free elections. Examples include Adolf Hitler and Joseph Stalin. For 10 points, name this form of government.

This word describes an authoritarian system that seeks to control every aspect of public and private life. Hannah Arendt wrote The Origins of this. For 10 points, name this system of Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union.

This international organization was formed in 1945 after World War II. It has a Security Council with five permanent members and a General Assembly. Its headquarters are in New York City. For 10 points, name this organization.

This military alliance was founded in 1949 by the United States, Canada, and ten European nations. An attack on one member is considered an attack on all. For 10 points, name this alliance with headquarters in Brussels.
This union of countries in Europe, created by the Maastricht Treaty, has a shared parliament and, for many members, a common currency, the euro. For 10 points, name this political and economic union.

This is the legislature in countries such as the United Kingdom, Canada, and India. In many such systems, the head of government is chosen from among its members. For 10 points, name this lawmaking body, whose House of Commons is an example.
In parliamentary systems, this official is the head of government, such as Winston Churchill or Justin Trudeau. For 10 points, name this position, whose title contains the word minister.

This word describes a legislature with two chambers. The United States Congress is an example, with the House and the Senate. Most American state legislatures except Nebraska are also of this type. For 10 points, give this term for a legislature with two chambers, the opposite of unicameral.

This term describes efforts by groups to influence government officials to make decisions that favor their interests. It is protected by the First Amendment right to petition. For 10 points, name this practice.

This is an organized group of people who share similar goals and try to win elections. In the United States, the two major ones are the Democrats and Republicans. For 10 points, name this type of group.

This is a direct vote by citizens on a single proposal or issue. Examples include the 2016 British vote on leaving the European Union. In Switzerland, citizens use these often, and some American states use similar ballot measures. For 10 points, name this type of vote.

This word describes the right to vote. The Nineteenth Amendment extended it to women, and the Fifteenth Amendment extended it to Black men. The Voting Rights Act of 1965 later enforced it. The Seneca Falls Convention of 1848 began the long movement for women to have it. For 10 points, name this right.

This practice of drawing district boundaries to favor one party takes its name from a Massachusetts governor and a salamander-shaped district. Redistricting happens after each census, and maps drawn this way can pack or crack voters. For 10 points, name this practice.

This Italian Renaissance writer wrote The Prince, advising rulers that it is safer to be feared than loved. His name now describes cunning and ruthless politics. For 10 points, name this man from Florence.
This document, sealed by King John in 1215, limited the power of the English monarchy and is seen as an early step toward constitutional government. For 10 points, name this charter.
